companies.title: Jim Dandy’s Transmissions
paragraphs: A business story that began with hard work.

Before the downtown buildings and festival crowds, Jim ran Jim Dandy’s Transmissions. A 2020 Oklahoma Gazette account names the transmission business among his early ventures, alongside four nightclubs in the 1970s. It is an early chapter in the entrepreneurial path that eventually led to Bricktown. [4]

companies.title: Super Rig Club
paragraphs: The Superrig. A doorway into nightlife.

The family’s chronology of Lackmeyer’s early-career profile recalls Jim backing an acquaintance’s nightclub, then taking over its operation. He discovered he enjoyed the business and welcomed guests at the door—a chapter that helped lead toward his later entertainment ventures. [18]
Also remembered as “The Superrig.” Exact opening and closing dates remain to be established.

companies.title: Brewer Enterprises
paragraphs: Another name behind the Bricktown years.

Oklahoma Gazette’s November 2008 remembrance identifies Jim as the owner of both Brewer Enterprises and Brewer Entertainment. Brewer Enterprises deserves its own place in the family history; the report does not establish its founding date or a separate inventory of its assets. [6]

companies.title: Bricktown Real Estate
paragraphs: The buildings behind the possibilities.

Downtown OKC’s board directory lists Brent Brewer with Bricktown Real Estate LLC. An earlier Greater Oklahoma City Chamber report identifies Bricktown Real Estate as the Santa Fe Depot’s owner and Brent as its president. Together, those records document another company in the family’s downtown story. [15] [16]

companies.title: Bricktown Live
paragraphs: A venue with a chapter of its own.

The Journal Record’s 2008 remembrance lists Bricktown Live among the properties purchased and managed by Brewer Entertainment. Oklahoma Gazette also names it among the venues operated by Jim’s businesses. These are historical accounts; the exact opening and closing dates remain to be established. [5] [6]

companies.title: Bricktown Ballroom
paragraphs: Another place to bring people together.

Bricktown Ballroom appears in both The Journal Record and Oklahoma Gazette’s 2008 accounts of the Brewer venue portfolio. It belongs alongside Bricktown Live and the event center in the entertainment history. These sources establish the Brewer connection, while its full operating timeline remains to be documented. [5] [6]

companies.title: Bricktown Haunted Warehouse
paragraphs: The attraction that helped start it all.

The Haunted Warehouse gave people a reason to visit Bricktown before the canal and ballpark. Retro Metro OKC traces its origins to Jim Brewer and Craig Brown seeing possibilities in the old Hunzicker Lighting building. A 2013 Brewer Entertainment release documents its later home at the Chevy Bricktown Events Center. [1] [3] [11]

companies.title: O’Brien’s Bricktown Club
paragraphs: An Irish pub. A new Bricktown tradition.

In a 2020 interview, Brent Brewer recalled opening O’Brien’s on March 17, 1990, alongside the St. Patrick’s Day parade and a block party in the parking lot. He said the pub operated for seven years. The celebration outlived the venue and became part of the family’s continuing story. [4]

companies.title: Brewer Entertainment
paragraphs: Turning places into experiences.

The Journal Record’s 2008 remembrance dates Brewer Entertainment Inc.’s start to 1991. At that time, it described a portfolio that included the Coca-Cola Bricktown Events Center, Bricktown Live, Bricktown Ballroom, and the Santa Fe train depot, alongside outdoor festivals. [5]

companies.title: Bricktown Parking
paragraphs: The practical side of welcoming a crowd.

Bricktown Parking belongs in the company history identified by the Brewer family. Public records also show why parking mattered to the district’s growth: the city’s 2008 parking strategy lists Jim Brewer among consulted stakeholders and Bricktown Parking Investors among contacted operators. [13]
The company’s founding date and the relationship between the differently named parking entities remain to be documented.

companies.title: Fourth of July festivals
paragraphs: Fireworks, music, and a city coming together.

A 2008 Oklahoma Gazette remembrance recounts the crowds at Bricktown’s 1999 Fourth of July fireworks after the canal opened. In 2007, the Gazette separately documented Brewer Entertainment’s Red, White and Boom! on the River—a free, three-day celebration at Downtown Airpark with the Oklahoma City Philharmonic and other performers. [6] [7]

companies.title: Bricktown Blues Fest
paragraphs: A soundtrack for summer in Bricktown.

The 2008 Gazette preview documents a two-day, free Blues & BBQ festival at Sheridan and Oklahoma avenues, with Marcia Ball, Bugs Henderson, and regional musicians. The family identifies Blues Fest as part of its history; the public account establishes the festival and lineup. [8]
An original program or company archive will help document the first year and full production credits.

companies.title: Bricktown Reggae Fest
paragraphs: A different rhythm for downtown.

The Journal Record reported in July 2014 that Brewer Entertainment had hosted Reggae Fest for 19 years. Its account describes a free event with performers including Watusi, Ugly Lion, and The Effinays, and an emphasis on bringing live entertainment to Bricktown. [9]

companies.title: Coca-Cola & Chevy Bricktown Events Center
paragraphs: Two names in one venue’s story.

A 2008 account places the Coca-Cola venue within Brewer Entertainment’s operations. Songkick identifies Chevy Bricktown Event Center as formerly the Coca-Cola Bricktown Event Center. Brewer Entertainment’s 2013 announcement documents the Chevy name and a Haunted Warehouse season at the venue. [5] [10] [11]
The precise sponsorship-change date is still to be established.

companies.title: Santa Fe Depot
paragraphs: Preserving a gateway to Oklahoma City.

Amtrak’s station history records Jim Brewer’s 1998 purchase of the depot and the renovation that followed. The Heartland Flyer began service in 1999. This chapter connects the family’s downtown work with the return of passenger rail to Oklahoma. [12]

companies.title: The Bricktown Okctopus
paragraphs: A new landmark on a familiar wall.

Oklahoma Tourism records Jack Fowler’s mural on the north side of the Chevy Bricktown Events Center in late 2016. The 200-foot-wide artwork made the building part of Bricktown’s public-art landscape. [14]

timeline.title: Where it all began
paragraphs: Jim D. Brewer is born February 6. His mother, Evelyn, raises him and his four sisters in southeast Oklahoma City by ironing clothes and sewing quilts. Jim is mowing lawns and doing odd jobs while still in grade school. [17]
timeline.evidence_note: Early-life detail from family-supplied chronology; dates approximate

timeline.title: Out on his own at 11
paragraphs: Jim leaves home to live with his grandfather near SE 28 and Central. He works until midnight at the Play More Bowling Alley at NW 4 and Broadway, walks miles home, and sleeps in the chicken coop so he doesn't break his grandfather's 5 a.m. breakfast rule. [17]
timeline.evidence_note: Early-life detail from family-supplied chronology; dates approximate

timeline.title: Jim Dandy's Transmissions
paragraphs: Working at an uncle's salvage yard, Jim learns to rebuild transmissions. After marrying and starting a family, he opens his own shop, Jim Dandy's Transmissions, on Reno near Harvey. [18]
timeline.evidence_note: Early-life detail from family-supplied chronology; dates approximate

timeline.title: The Superrig
paragraphs: Jim backs an acquaintance who wants to buy a nightclub, then takes it over when his partner can't run it. He finds he loves the business and greets every guest at the door. [18]
timeline.evidence_note: Early-life detail from family-supplied chronology; dates approximate

timeline.title: Striking oil
paragraphs: Like much of Oklahoma during the boom, Jim buys an oil well. The first is a bust, but the second does very well. [18]
timeline.evidence_note: Early-life detail from family-supplied chronology; dates approximate

timeline.title: The Tom Cat well
paragraphs: Jim’s recollection describes the Tom Cat well in western Oklahoma bringing in $600,000 in a single day. He leaves the nightclub life, sells his oil interests near the peak, and buys workover rigs, staying profitable through the subsequent oil downturn. [18]
timeline.evidence_note: Early-life detail from family-supplied chronology; dates approximate

timeline.title: Called to Bricktown
paragraphs: Looking for someone to carry on founding developer Neal Horton's work, his partner Williams turns to Jim for his cash and toughness. Jim starts buying warehouses from banks eager to sell. [19]
timeline.evidence_note: Early-life detail from family-supplied chronology; dates approximate

timeline.title: A warehouse becomes a destination
paragraphs: Jim and Craig Brown see an opportunity in an old warehouse. The Bricktown Haunted Warehouse opens, giving people a reason to visit a district still finding its new identity. [1] [3]
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: Restaurants bring new momentum
paragraphs: Spaghetti Warehouse opens. Its crowds help establish demand for dining and entertainment among Bricktown’s old buildings. [3]
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: O’Brien’s & St. Patrick’s Day
paragraphs: Brent recalls opening O’Brien’s on March 17 alongside the parade and the first parking-lot block party. The pub and the celebration become part of the family story. [4]
Family recollection: Patsy sold T-shirts at O’Brien’s.
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: Brewer Entertainment takes shape
paragraphs: Jim starts Brewer Entertainment Inc., bringing venues and outdoor festivals into a growing entertainment business. [5]
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: Planning the canal together
paragraphs: Lackmeyer and Jack Money report on the public-private partnership behind the MAPS canal project, including Jim’s involvement as a Bricktown property owner. The Oklahoman ↗
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: A new chapter for the depot
paragraphs: Jim purchases the Santa Fe Depot. Restoration helps prepare the historic station for the return of passenger rail. [12]
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: The canal opens. The crowds arrive.
paragraphs: The Bricktown Canal opens in July, and the Heartland Flyer brings passenger service back to the depot. Recollections of the Fourth of July describe more than 50,000 people gathering for fireworks. [12] [6]
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: Red, White and Boom! on the River
paragraphs: Brewer Entertainment promotes a free, three-day Fourth of July celebration at Downtown Airpark, with the Oklahoma City Philharmonic and other performers. Contemporary coverage previews the planned event. Oklahoma Gazette ↗
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: A summer soundtrack
paragraphs: Contemporary festival coverage previews Bricktown Blues & BBQ, with Marcia Ball, Bugs Henderson, and regional musicians. Live music remains part of the district’s summer identity. [8]
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: Jim tells the rest of his story
paragraphs: The Oklahoman’s June video profile and Lackmeyer’s June 29 articles explore Jim’s early life, career, and the different views of his role in Bricktown. The Oklahoman Video Archive ↗ The Oklahoman ↗
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: Remembering Jim
paragraphs: Jim dies on November 11. Family remembrance and local reporting reflect on his life, his businesses, and his role in Bricktown’s renewal. [2] [5]
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: A place in the Walk of Fame
paragraphs: Lackmeyer reports on Walk of Fame recognition for Bricktown’s early developers, including Jim. The district’s public record begins a new chapter of remembrance. The Oklahoman ↗
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: The Haunted Warehouse at Chevy
paragraphs: A Brewer Entertainment announcement documents the attraction’s 28th annual season at the Chevy Bricktown Events Center on California Avenue. [11]
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: Another chapter for the event center
paragraphs: Lackmeyer reports on planned Chevy Bricktown Events Center renovations aimed at attracting performers. The venue remains part of the family’s entertainment story. The Oklahoman ↗
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: Reggae Fest becomes a tradition
paragraphs: The Journal Record reports that Brewer Entertainment has hosted Reggae Fest for 19 years. The free festival brings performers and crowds together, alongside the practical challenges of producing outdoor events. [9]
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: Renovating in Jim’s honor
paragraphs: The Journal Record covers Brent and Brett’s plans to bring new life to the former Haunted Warehouse buildings as a tribute to their father. The Journal Record ↗
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: A new landmark on a familiar wall
paragraphs: Jack Fowler’s Bricktown Okctopus mural takes shape on the event-center wall. The large artwork becomes another recognizable part of the district. [14]
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: New events. A continuing tradition.
paragraphs: Lackmeyer’s Bricktown Throwdown coverage connects the athletic competition to Brett and Brent’s event business and the district’s tradition of bringing people together. The Oklahoman ↗
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: The sons carry the story forward
paragraphs: A November Lackmeyer feature follows Brent and Brett continuing to develop and invest in the places associated with their father’s legacy. The Oklahoman ↗
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

timeline.title: Thirty years of St. Patrick’s Day
paragraphs: A Gazette interview recalls O’Brien’s 1990 opening and three decades of block parties. Brent describes the brothers’ continuing work and plans to dedicate that year’s celebration to Jim. [4]
timeline.evidence_note: Published sources and identified family recollections

articles.title: Bricktown rides antique shuttle
articles.summary: Jim Brewer supported a proposed antique-car shuttle linking downtown parking with Bricktown. The report captures parking pressure and the push to diversify the district beyond nightlife.

articles.title: City Beat: Schwartz elected president
articles.summary: A brief mention places Jim Brewer on an Oklahoma City delegation to San Antonio and credits his influence on the proposed canal alignment along California Street.

articles.title: Depot renovation begins for return of Amtrak
articles.summary: Coverage of approved federal funding and restoration preparations at the Santa Fe Depot. Jim Brewer discussed the work needed before passenger rail service returned.

articles.title: Restoring our gateway
articles.summary: Jim and Brent Brewer’s plans for the Santa Fe Depot combined passenger facilities with preservation of its Art Deco character. This is a contemporary account of the restoration effort.

articles.title: OKC gets rail passenger link to Texas
articles.summary: An account of preparations for renewed passenger service, including Brewer Enterprises’ restoration work at the Santa Fe Depot.

articles.title: Bricktown: a hub of Oklahoma City history
articles.summary: A canal-opening-era history of the warehouse district describes Jim Brewer’s property investments during the 1980s within Bricktown’s broader redevelopment story.

articles.title: Heartland Flyer anniversary preparations
articles.summary: A preview of the train’s first-anniversary celebrations mentions Jim Brewer hosting a special luncheon. The article documents plans rather than confirming every event occurred.

articles.title: Pioneering Bricktown
articles.summary: Looks back at early investment and entertainment in Bricktown, including Jim Brewer’s involvement from 1985. It also recognizes the other developers and businesses involved in the district’s revival.

articles.title: Bricktown construction booms
articles.summary: Jim Brewer discusses the effect of MAPS investment and new construction. The report also describes uneven weekday activity as the entertainment district continued to develop.

articles.title: Jim and Patsy Brewer parking-lot sale
articles.summary: A property-transactions roundup reports Jim and Patsy Brewer selling a parking lot near Sheridan and Joe Carter for a proposed Bricktown Market Place development. The apartment sale in the original headline is a separate transaction.

articles.title: Celebrate the Fourth at Red, White and Boom!
articles.summary: C.J. Macklin previews Brewer Entertainment’s free, three-day celebration with the Oklahoma City Philharmonic and other performers. This event was at Downtown Airpark, separate from Bricktown’s earlier fireworks celebrations.

articles.title: These Walls: Santa Fe Station
articles.summary: Traces the station’s architecture and later uses, including Jim Brewer’s 1998 purchase, restoration, and the return of passenger service in 1999.

articles.title: Bricktown’s 13th annual blues festival
articles.summary: Jake Dalton previews the free Blues & BBQ event at Sheridan and Oklahoma avenues, featuring Marcia Ball, Bugs Henderson, and regional musicians. This report documents the festival and lineup; it does not establish the complete production credits.

articles.title: Bricktown Comprehensive Parking Strategy
articles.summary: The city’s parking study lists Jim Brewer among consulted stakeholders and Bricktown Parking Investors among contacted operators. It documents district parking conditions; it does not by itself establish the relationship between every similarly named parking business.

articles.title: Bricktown pioneer Jim Brewer dies
articles.summary: Remembers Jim Brewer’s investments, venues, festivals, and prominent role in Bricktown. Alongside tributes, the account describes a strong personality and disagreements with others involved in the district.

articles.title: Jim Brewer obituary
articles.summary: The family obituary recounts Jim’s early businesses, oil ventures, and work in Bricktown. Originally published November 12–13, 2008, it provides a family remembrance alongside independent newspaper coverage.

articles.title: Bricktown merchant mourns district pioneer
articles.summary: Scott Cooper records Jim Cowan’s memories of Brewer, the merchants’ association, and major crowds at the 1999 Fourth of July celebration. It connects the events to Bricktown’s changing fortunes.

articles.title: “Mayor of Bricktown” dies
articles.summary: A remembrance of Jim Brewer’s business career and the entertainment ventures that helped bring visitors into the warehouse district.

articles.title: Coca-Cola Bricktown Events Center directory entry
articles.summary: The 2008 venue guide lists Brewer Entertainment with the Coca-Cola Bricktown Events Center at 425 California. This contemporaneous industry record helps document the venue’s earlier name.

articles.title: Bricktown merchants hold talks on future
articles.summary: A Chamber-hosted newspaper report covers merchants’ discussions about Bricktown’s next phase, including plans to honor early contributors such as Neal Horton and Jim Brewer.
articles.author: Steve Lackmeyer

articles.title: Alea London v. Canal Club
articles.publisher: Oklahoma Court of Civil Appeals / Justia
articles.summary: An insurance-coverage appeal arising from an intoxicated-driver injury case. The opinion records that claims against Brewer Entertainment and Bricktown Canal Properties were dismissed without prejudice before the underlying trial.
articles.context: The appeal concerned coverage for a judgment against Canal Club, not a liability finding against the Brewer companies. The appellate court reversed and remanded for judgment in the insurer’s favor. Dismissal without prejudice is not a decision on the merits.

articles.title: Santa Fe Station’s hidden architecture
articles.summary: Ben Fenwick examines a long-hidden tunnel beneath the tracks and the station’s potential as a transportation hub. Brent Brewer discusses the building as city planning work continues.

articles.title: Oklahoma officials reach Amtrak pact
articles.summary: An AP report describes a station-use agreement following locked-door incidents that required alternative arrangements for passengers. Brent Brewer said repeated requests for a new lease had gone unanswered.
articles.context: The report documents a subsequent agreement with the state. Summary is based on indexed text of the newspaper preserved by Texas Tech’s archive.

articles.title: The Rising
articles.summary: Lindsey Johnson explores Oklahoma City’s urban renewal and MAPS-era development. Jim Brewer’s entertainment investments appear within the larger story of downtown’s transformation.

articles.title: Western World Insurance v. Markel American Insurance
articles.publisher: U.S. Court of Appeals, Tenth Circuit / Justia
articles.summary: The opinion describes an employee’s fall down an elevator shaft at the Bricktown Haunted House and the resulting suit against Brewer Entertainment. The injury suit had already settled; this appeal concerned the insurers’ responsibility for costs.
articles.context: The court reversed summary judgment for Markel and remanded. This was an insurance-allocation decision, not a new injury judgment against Brewer Entertainment.

articles.title: Bass pros and cons
articles.summary: A debate over government incentives for retail development includes Brent Brewer’s support for anchor stores and cautions about public subsidies. The disagreement concerns development policy.

articles.title: Festival of the foods
articles.summary: Greg Elwell’s Festival of the Arts food coverage includes Brewer Entertainment’s brisket sales. It documents food operations at the Arts Council’s festival, rather than crediting Brewer with producing the entire event.

articles.title: Mystery train
articles.summary: Jerry Bohnen reports on the city’s effort to acquire the Santa Fe Depot and a sharp gap between the owner’s asking price and the city’s offer. The article captures an unresolved acquisition dispute at that time.

articles.title: Grant and valuation move transit hub forward
articles.summary: A follow-up covers federal grant funding and a reported $4.5 million depot valuation in the condemnation process. This is a dated account of that process, not a statement of the final acquisition price.

articles.title: The Scare is Everywhere Inside the Bricktown Haunted Warehouse
articles.summary: Brewer Entertainment announces the attraction’s 28th annual season at the Pepsi Chevy Bricktown Events Center, 425 California. This company-issued release documents the venue name and advertised season.

articles.title: Seeing red, gold and green
articles.summary: Caele Pemberton reports on Brewer Entertainment’s long-running free Reggae Fest. Alongside performers and community appeal, the account discusses weather risk and years when the event lost money.

articles.title: New life for haunted house site
articles.summary: Molly M. Fleming covers Brent and Brett Brewer’s building renovations honoring Jim. The article also describes debate over electronic signs and advertising rules in the historic district.
articles.context: Renovation approval and unresolved sign questions are separate issues. The report does not establish a final denial of every Brewer sign proposal.

articles.title: The scare house that helped revive a warehouse district
articles.summary: Brett Fieldcamp interviews Brent Brewer about the Haunted Warehouse’s origins, its early crowds, and the creative work behind its scares. Recollections and attendance figures are presented as the interviewee’s account.

articles.title: Reggaefest becomes a summertime tradition
articles.summary: Ben Luschen previews the festival’s 21st edition and interviews Brent Brewer about its free, all-ages format and place in Bricktown’s summer calendar.

articles.title: Debating the Bricktown octopus mural
articles.summary: Patrick’s commentary examines criticism and changing responses to Jack Fowler’s octopus mural, a project supported by the Brewers and Downtown OKC Initiatives. It is included as an opinion piece, rather than an objective verdict on the artwork.

articles.title: Wormy Dog Saloon to close its doors
articles.summary: Jacob McCleland and Ted Streuli discuss the venue’s closure. The account says Levelland Productions chose not to renew its lease with property owner Brewer Entertainment; Brent Brewer was assessing the building’s future.

articles.title: Alcoholmanac: Spirited tradition
articles.summary: Matt Dinger interviews Brent Brewer about O’Brien’s March 17, 1990 opening and the family’s St. Patrick’s Day tradition. Its 2020 event plans are a preview, not confirmation that the celebration took place.

articles.title: Bricktown funding request
articles.summary: Brent Brewer calls for more funding as Bricktown grows.

articles.title: Bricktown Collection
articles.summary: A collection of photographs and district history, including family-contributed material and the work of multiple early developers. A starting point for placing the Brewer story in its wider setting.

articles.title: Bricktown history
articles.summary: The district’s history page describes its warehouse origins and early entertainment attractions, including the Haunted Warehouse associated with Jim Brewer.

articles.title: Oklahoma City Santa Fe Depot
articles.summary: The station history documents the depot’s architecture, Jim Brewer’s 1998 purchase, and the return of passenger rail service in 1999.

articles.title: Bricktown Okctopus mural
articles.summary: The state tourism listing identifies Jack Fowler’s large Bricktown octopus mural. It provides a descriptive record alongside the archive’s coverage of public reactions to the artwork.

articles.title: Bricktown parking debate stirs up
articles.publisher: The Oklahoman / copy preserved on OKCTalk
articles.summary: A newspaper article attributed to Steve Lackmeyer describes merchants’ complaints about parking prices and control of public lots. The copied report says Jim Brewer declined comment, while the Bricktown Association argued that cheaper parking options needed better publicity.
articles.context: The surviving copy was posted July 21, 2007; the original publisher page was not located. The city’s 2008 parking study independently identifies this article and the related discussion. This entry summarizes the attributed newspaper text, not forum replies.
articles.author: Steve Lackmeyer (attributed in preserved copy)
